consensus_summary: The new moon is the biblical monthly festival and calendrical marker initiating the lunar month, commonly associated with the dark conjunction or first visible crescent. In Christian theology, it is typically viewed as a ceremonial shadow fulfilled typologically in Christ.
book_summary: The biblical 'new moon' that marks the start of the month is actually the full moon in the east gate, directly rejecting the common view that it is the dark conjunction or first visible crescent.
consensus_core_identification: A monthly calendrical and ceremonial observance tied to the start of the lunar cycle (dark or crescent moon).
book_core_identification: The full moon in the east gate, marking the start of the appointed times and the month.
boundary_disagreement: The book completely reassigns the lunar phase that constitutes a 'new moon' and begins the month, moving it from the beginning of the visible lunar cycle to its peak (the full moon).
material_contradiction: The book asserts that the 'new moon' is the full moon, explicitly denying the established consensus and historical view that it is the dark conjunction or first visible crescent.
rationale: By identifying the 'new moon' as the full moon, the book fundamentally changes the physical referent of the term and the anchor point for the biblical calendar, resulting in a material contradiction with the consensus.
strongest_objection: The provided verses describe activities and worship that take place on the new moon and mention the east gate (Ezekiel 46), but none of the plain texts explicitly identify the new moon as the full moon. The historical and linguistic consensus strongly supports the crescent or dark moon as the start of the biblical month.
